articles.title: England vs Pakistan: 'Chickens come home to roost' for PCB as 'dismal' batting sees tourists bowled out within 34 overs in final Test
articles.summary: Pakistan's crisis-hit series against England worsened on day one of the third Test when they were bowled out for 133 within 34 overs; the third Test between England and Pakistan, at Edgbaston, continues live on Sky Sports on Thursday, September 10
articles.body:
"Unprecedented" was the word used by Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton to describe the upheaval that has occurred over the last week in response to heavy losses at Headingley and Lords.

Seven players were sent home, head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul were replaced, and an investigation began into "media reports concerning discipline and conduct".

If those actions were aimed at provoking a response, the Pakistan Cricket Board did not get the one it would have been after on day one at Edgbaston.

On the eve of the third Test, Root dismissed suggestions that Pakistan have shown "no fight" in the series as disrespectful to both teams.

But after four hours of day one Josh Tongue (4-42), Ollie Robinson (3-15), and Jofra Archer (3-25) had cleaned them up with relative ease.

By over 10, Pakistan were four down with just 29 runs on the board. It took England 11 more overs to take three more wickets, Pakistan posting just 71 more runs by lunch with a dismal 110-7 on the board.

Things were wrapped up by the 34th over, a total of 133 all the visitors could muster on what was described in the Sky Sports commentary box as a "blameless" pitch. It has been a low-scoring summer, but this was low even by those standards.

But was any other outcome expected? Or was the display delivered actually the most likely amid an extremely testing set of circumstances.

"A thoroughly miserable batting performance from them," said Atherton.

"It is a batting line-up woefully low on confidence, " he later added.

"The decision to send seven players home - the chickens are coming home to roost. You cannot treat players like that and expect to build confidence in a side.

"Everybody who plays professional sport knows that if you play badly, the axe is going to fall.

"For all the criticism that has been made, just bear the context in mind that this Pakistan team looks dispirited - and there is a reason for that."

Pakistan's issues have been laid bare, and it is not going to be a quick fix. If they lose this, they will have one victory in their last seven Tests.

Couple that with the clear unrest and more upheaval seems almost inevitable.

"When I saw what happened, you could almost not see where the inspiration would come from - with the skill, the experience, and the alien conditions," said Sky Sports Cricket's Urooj Mumtaz.

"But to top all of it, the turbulent conditions and the manner in which [the changes were made to the side].

"Underwhelming, absolutely no competition, and this is the worst we've seen so far."

'Impossible' to play good cricket with off-field turmoil

So was it too big an ask of Pakistan to even muster up a semblance of fight?

Sky Sports Cricket's Stuart Broad said: "It looks like a really difficult environment to play in.

"You often talk about playing with freedom, playing without fear but the worst place you can be is feeling you need 20 or 30 runs to stay in the team - you never warm together as a group.

"It's really impossible to play good cricket when you have that many off-field problems going."

Pakistan find solace in debutant Razaullah

England ended day one with a narrow lead of 23 runs after losing four wickets. Two of them came from "bright spark" Razaullah (2-42), who provided Pakistan with some hope on his debut.

The 21-year-old hit speeds of over 90mph and took the key wicket of Joe Root to reinvigorate his team and show that the future of Pakistan cricket still has potential.

On day two, it will be about whether the youngster can continue his strong showing with ball in hand to make his side's poor batting performance count for as little as possible.

"Pakistan have been calling out for something different from their bowlers for a long while," said Sky Sports Cricket's Nasser Hussain.

"It is nice to watch that spell from Razaullah that had something, that had a point of difference, had some pace.

"It hurried one of the greatest batters there has ever been in Joe Root, and got him out."

England vs Pakistan - results and schedule

First Test (Headingley) - England won by innings and 103 runs

Second Test (Lord's) - England won by 194 runs

articles.title: Emilio Gay: England batter has 'done enough' to retain spot for South Africa tour - Sir Alastair Cook
articles.summary: England batter Emilio Gay has done enough to lock in an opener's spot for their winter tour of South Africa, according to Sir Alastair Cook.
articles.body:
England opener Emilio Gay should retain his spot for their winter tour of South Africa, according to former captain Sir Alastair Cook.

Gay made a Test-best 60 from 114 balls to blunt Pakistan's attack which helped England seize control on day one at Edgbaston.

The 26-year-old left-hander's tally of 261 runs, at an average of 26.1, might not look particularly eye-catching.

But in an English summer where ball has dominated bat - Ben Duckett is England's only centurion in six home Tests so far - the Durham left-hander has shown a willingness to grind it out.

Cook, who made almost 12,000 runs as an opener for England, has been impressed with the character the Durham left-hander has shown to make tough runs at the top of the order.

"I think Emilio Gay's played really nicely. I would say he's confident and intense," Cook told Test Match Special.

"He is definitely a run-getter when he gets in. He seems to have that real stubborn and strong will to make it count if he can.

"He has done enough for me to take him to South Africa to continue the progress of a player where the pitches will be slightly easier to bat on and he should open the batting."

According to CricViz, Gay has left or defended 61% of the pace deliveries he's faced since his debut against New Zealand in June.

Dom Sibley in 2020 (68% left or defended) was the last English opener to register a higher percentage in a home summer.

During his innings on Wednesday, Gay left or defended 65 deliveries and Cook "likes how late he defends the ball" with a patient approach to more attacking strokeplay.

Gay scored the first 12 runs of his half-century off 43 balls before his next 38 came off 52 balls.

He hit nine fours and has scored 68% of his Test runs in boundaries - the joint-highest of any England batter with at least 250 runs in the red-ball format.

"If you take Gay's innings, and what I've seen of him, he's not hunting that drive too often. He waits for it to come into there," added Cook.

"He scores off the back foot through the off side as well. He scored through the leg side and timed them through mid-wicket so he does have an all-round game. He's not limited to the off side."

Given Pakistan's flimsy batting - bowled out for 133 in their first innings here - it could end up being Gay's final Test innings of the summer.

With Jacob Bethell set to return for the tour of South Africa following injury, the selection of a top-order batter for the winter is likely to be a scrap between Jordan Cox, Dan Lawrence and Gay for two places.

Only Harry Brook (six occasions) has passed 30 more times than Gay (five) during a challenging summer for batters.

Although Gay has struggled to play back of a length bowling with seven dismissals in the 7-9 metre length range which has highlighted a potential weakness.

Former England captain Michael Vaughan said Gay "played nicely" but might reflect on an missed opportunity to reach three figures for the first time after he dragged on a delivery from Razaullah Khan.

"Emilio Gay found his balance early. He had it hard at the start and then he found his flow," Vaughan said.

"He'll be really disappointed to get out for 60. He'll be desperate to get his first Test match century and I thought it was on today.

"That extra little bit of pace from Razaullah and a little lack of concentration at the end of the day has cost him."

England seamer Josh Tongue said Gay's rigorous preparation has helped him develop the necessary powers of concentration for Test cricket.

"The one thing I've seen in Emilio is he trains really hard in the nets. He'll bat for ages, putting a lot of hard work in, and it's shown on the pitch," added Tongue.

"Even last week at Lord's, he had two quite horrible dismissals, but I felt today he batted unbelievable on a tricky pitch.

"He was obviously really disappointed with how he got out. It's not a nice feeling, chopping on, but he's put the team in a really good position for tomorrow."
